original_text: Cheap implementation has another consequence: agents can produce unnecessary complexity at extraordinary speed. In my experience, coding agents readily introduce abstractions, architectural layers, and mechanisms that are reasonable in isolation but inappropriate for the system at hand. A design pattern may be sound, yet add more machinery than the problem warrants; a general solution may accommodate cases the system will never encounter. Empirical studies of AI-generated changes identify overengineering and poor contextual fit as reasons for rejection or reversion\citep{oukhay2026aicodedoesntstick,ogenrwot2026patchtrack}. Agents can also explain and defend these choices convincingly. The engineer must judge whether the proposed structure fits the actual requirements, existing architecture, and likely evolution of the system. Parsimony is therefore an active engineering responsibility: deciding not only whether a design works, but whether its complexity is justified.

Agents can also explain and defend these choices convincingly. The engineer must judge whether the proposed structure fits the actual requirements, existing architecture, and likely evolution of the system. Parsimony is therefore an active engineering responsibility: deciding not only whether a design works, but whether its complexity is justified.

Much of my work with agents comes down to deciding what is an implementation detail and what is not. I generally do not care what a variable is called or how an ordinary function is organized, provided the result satisfies its obligations. I do care whether the implementation crosses an architectural boundary, introduces a new dependency, or changes the behavior of a service that other components rely on. The difficulty is that these distinctions are not always apparent in advance. Sometimes an agent makes a perfectly reasonable choice, I look at the result, and discover that I care about something I had never thought to specify. That is part of engineering. The next step is to decide whether the newly discovered obligation should become explicit, so that future work does not have to discover it again.

original_text:
I have found that this process develops the engineer as well as the system. One fear about increasingly capable machines is that engineers will lose expertise as machines perform more of the work. That can happen if delegation removes the engineer from the feedback through which expertise develops. My experience with MAGE has been nearly the opposite. Cheap realization creates the realization amplification described in \magevalue{chapter:one-problem-many-models}: I can form a hypothesis, model it, realize it, measure what happens, discover where my understanding was wrong, and repeat the cycle many times in the time a conventional implementation might once have taken. That compressed exploration also produces connection amplification. Consequences that conventional development might have separated by days or weeks arrive close enough together for their relationships to become visible.

The learning does not accrue only to the environment. The engineer goes through the loop too. Repeatedly choosing representations, confronting predictions with evidence, finding the proper level of a failure, and deciding what knowledge should become durable machinery forces the engineer to learn. Abundant implementation can deskill an engineer who merely consumes its output; used this way, it can instead become an unusually powerful medium for developing engineering judgment.

original_text: Most readers do not begin on a blank page. You inherit code, tests, schemas, architectural documents, CI rules, permissions, dashboards, conventions, and operational lore. Some of that inheritance is debt; some is useful engineering structure that has become fragmented, stale, or difficult to reuse. Brownfield engineering is therefore partly an exercise in recovery: find the representations and controls the system already owns, reconnect them to the territory they describe, repair or retire what has drifted, and invest in new structure where recurring engineering costs justify it.

Most readers do not begin on a blank page. You inherit code, tests, schemas, architectural documents, CI rules, permissions, dashboards, conventions, and operational lore. Some of that inheritance is debt; some is useful engineering structure that has become fragmented, stale, or difficult to reuse. Brownfield engineering is therefore partly an exercise in recovery: find the representations and controls the system already owns, reconnect them to the territory they describe, repair or retire what has drifted, and invest in new structure where recurring engineering costs justify it.

The objective is not to model the entire existing system before agents can work on it. It is to make the next consequential change safely, then improve the engineering environment so that later changes become easier to govern. Existing tests, permissions, architecture documents, and review practices are starting points. Some already enforce useful obligations; others depend on someone remembering what to check. The work is to discover which is which, establish what can be trusted, and strengthen the environment one important property at a time.

original_text: Process design and tolerance help explain the different arrangements observed in this chapter (\autoref{process-design-and-tolerance}). DocAble\textquotesingle s accessibility obligations and one-engineer staffing made explicit requirements and automated rejection especially valuable: I had little inherited human process to accommodate and no spare reviewers for every implementation decision. Coordinating agents still required work orders, scheduling, and completion checks. In an established organization, the factory must also fit existing teams, knowledge, and authority. Both settings require judgments about which properties to preserve and how to organize work around them. A more capable agent may change the process needed to produce a system without changing its memory bound or deployment restriction. Engineers can leave implementation choices open within those bounds, while weighing the cost of supervision against the cost of maintaining the representations and checks that support it.

Organizations need not begin with fully autonomous implementation. Some use agents to review pull requests or propose changes that people still inspect. Others allow agents to implement and validate changes before routing selected decisions to human reviewers. These arrangements delegate different amounts of work and authority, but they face the same engineering questions: what must remain true, what evidence establishes it, and which decisions require human approval? MAGE applies to those questions even when most implementation remains under direct human supervision.
